69. Oecus (p), floor and wall N. Mosaic and painting also underline the partition between a front, more richly decorated and vaulted, with a coffered floor and megalographies on the walls, and a simpler interior covered perhaps flat, with a mosaic floor of white tesserae arranged in an oblique warp and faux marble paintings. A two-strand braid arranged in a Greek cross borders and highlights the five central coffers of the antechamber floor, all different, while a chest of drawers with a perspective motif is repeated at the four corners. A strip adorned with a branch on the floor, and a pillar on the walls connect the two parts of the room. II style, phase II a.

76. Oecus (p), wall N of the antechamber. —Megalography with a philosopher seated in front of the globe of the universe and traces of the figure of Urania at the left end. 77. Oecus(p), wall E, antechamber and hall. The megalograph of the antechamber here houses the exotic figuration that has given the room the name of the Hall of the Elephants: a pair of elephants looks out of a low podium framed by ovoli and arrows, on either side of a tall candelabrum, each led by a pair of cupids with floral reins. The figuration has been interpreted as alluding to the power of Venus. Beyond a dividing pillar continues the simplest decoration of the room which, above a sort of wooden case, has a row of ashlars and high purple orthostats. II style, phase II a. 15 AFSC734

78. Oecus (p), O wall, antechamber and hall. In the room, the faux marble figuration echoes that of the wall in front, while the megalography of the antechamber represents Clio seated. II style, phase II a. The small door in the corner leads to the annex, small cubicle in red monochrome. The continuous construction of the S wall of the two rooms can be distinguished, left to rough plaster; it is a consequence of the division of the single original complex onto which the rooms (P), (Q) and (S) opened, now transformed into the public triclinium (16) of House I 6, 2, pp. 197-200, figs. 4-12.77 N35334

80. Cubicle (q), black and white mosaic floor with the use of polychrome tiles. The carpet of the antechamber is adorned with a network of hexagons; in the center, within a border of ivy shoots, was placed the emblem executed in the workshop on a terracotta support, removed in antiquity. In the bedside rug, circles and squares with concave sides. II style, phase II a.

82-83. Cubicle (q), wall E with the door communicating with the Hall of the Elephants (p). The only note that interrupts the monochrome of the red walls, in imitation of porphyry, is given by the faux green marble pillar, which is imagined to be adorned with gems set, and which separates the alcove from the antechamber. In the two parts of the room, the decoration is based on the incrustation of large red orthostats, above which appear in the alcove paintings imitating colored marble reliefs, while in the antechamber there is a rich series of friezes and frames, with perspective meandering, with shoots, weapons and Nereids riding seahorses. The room, of very small dimensions, is therefore loaded with a complicated decoration of great perspective effect, rich and refined, with which the reduced polychromy of the floor is in agreement, played not only on black and white, but also on red and green. II style, phase II a.

2 a-b. Retrobottega (n), wall E. Until the earthquake of 62 A.D. the back of the shop, which previously served as a triclinium in the adjoining house, was accessible - at least after the repainting in the third style - only from the cubicle (1), with which it shares the type of black solid background decoration. 7. Atrium (b), impluvium seen from O. The bottom of the ancient tuff impluvium with shaped edges has been reinforced with a layer of cocciopesto, in which white mosaic tiles and geometrically shaped tiles (circles, diamonds, squares and rectangles, triangles and fractions of the same) of colored marble are densely inserted. Apart from a few diamonds of palombino (7 cm on each side) from a republican floor of scutulata, there is an almost complete sample of colored marbles imported from Greece and Africa available in the first century AD: Numidian, ancient red, portasanta, African, cipollino, breccia di Aleppo. The bardiglio and white marble tiles come from Carrara. 77 N35076

On the shelf supported by the lion's head, left rough to hold the table, is engraved in purely republican characters the name of the former owner P. CASCA LOIN]G perhaps that P. Servilius, tribunus plebis, who first struck Caesar in the Senate on the Ides of March (Suet., Caes., 82.1; Pliut, Caes., 66.2; App., Rom., 2.492). The murderer's property was confiscated by Octavian; the fact that the table supports ended up in Pompeii, means that there was some link between one of the inhabitants of the house and the central power of Rome. This would also explain the quality of the paintings.

17. Atrium (b), N-W corner. A paratactic wall system with light blue panels separated by black pilasters with floral candelabra had been applied to the atrium. In the center of the panels there was a painting with a theatrical subject, ten in total; The alternation of tragic and comic scenes that occurs in the gallery of paintings would also reflect the alternation of public and private which is a fundamental aspect of life in the atrium. 21. Atrium(b), wall O, section N, middle area, second panel from N, detail: painting summarizing a scene from the new comedy, in which a male figure with tousled hair protruding behind his ears, argues with a cook seated at the high tripod with a globular container. The latter corresponds to mask no. 25 in Pollux's catalogue (Onomastikòn, 4, 150); the patowv with a bald skull and a mass of hair all around the height of the ears. We probably witness the scene of Demeas who, in the presence of the cook, extorts a testimony from the slave Parmenon with the threat of the whip and the mark with the hot iron, from the comedy Samìa (455-495) by Menander. At the end of the act Parmenon melts away and perhaps, for this reason, only half a figure appears, cut from the frame of the painting.

20. Atrium (b), O wall, N section, middle area, N pilaster, detail. The upper section of the floral candelabrum includes two facing Pegasi, a Delphic tripod, and the stem all covered with leaves from which three tragic masks are hung recognizable by the éykoc, the tall wig. The lower section of the candelabrum, which has the same structure, is best read on the N pilaster of the E wall.

22. Atrium (b), N wall, O section, middle area, detail. The wardrobe set up in the N-W corner cut off the lower section of the comic painting depicting the Lykomedèios, Pollux's mask No. '7 (Onomastikòn 4.144): an old man with a curled beard, raising an eyebrow with an intriguing air.

27. Atrium (b), wall E, section N, middle area, pilaster N, detail. The lower section of the candelabrum is composed of a chalice-like base with a white marble acanthus tuft, from which shoots sprout ending in purple flowers with yellow (golden) corolla and pistil, at the feet of two leaning hawks, with outstretched wings, also of white marble, which act as caryatids to a silver ring turned around the porphyry stem; above two overlapping golden chalices there are three masks hanging from the stem all covered with leaves and golden apples (yellow) picked by Heracles in the garden of the Hesperides. The garden of the golden apples is located in the center of the world, indicated by the omphalòs (navel) sacred to Gaia, covered by the mantic net and surmounted by the yellow Delphic tripod (of gilded bronze) of A pollo; on the purple background between the feet of the tripod hangs the vannus (basket/cradle) of Dionysus Liknites. The tripod is flanked by thyrsis delimiting a red field. The black background of the pilaster expresses the chthonic and mysterious character of Dionysus. The Thyiades (from Thyias, the first Maenad) of Delphi celebrated the resurrection of the child in the cradle (liknon) in winter, on Parnassus, according to Plutarch (Mor., 365A) in a passage that explains the Osiris-Dionysus assimilation believed in Delphi. The Egyptian touch shines through in the two falcons of Horus at the base of the stem: symbols of the divine Egyptian royalty (of Upper and Lower Egypt), but here used to support the winner's trophy with their wings. The light strikes from the right on the candelabrum, in correspondence with the source of natural light in the atrium, i.e. the compluvium.

The tragic scene probably represents the moment after the blinding of Polymestor by Hecuba to avenge the killing of his younger son Polydorus: the latter, to save the gold of Troy, had been sent in secret by Priam to his friend Polymestor, king of the Thracian Chersonese. He kills his two sons under the tent and blinds the king. The moment captured in the picture would be that of Polymestor's lament as he came out of the tent, exclaiming: "Woe to me, where I go, where I put myself" (Eur., Hekàbe, 1056-1057). Bakyarg èidov, "Infernal Bacchae, possessed by murderous fury", calls Hecuba and companions (Hekàbe, 1077). Blind, he becomes clairvoyant and reveals the fatal fate of Hecuba and her daughter Cassandra.

44. Cubicle (2), ceiling, S-E section. The cubicle was treated by the decorator as a cave with a view of the sky: through the openings in the ceiling you can observe the firmament marked by Venus, the evening star. In all probability cubicles (1) and (2) were still communicating at the time of the decoration in the III style; then the solid black background of (1) could be the background to the necessary initiation of the user to pass to the paradisiacal state in the flowery cave of the cubicle (2). The ceiling of the latter is articulated like that of a flooded roof, surrounded by a perforated coffered in turn in the center of each coffered ceiling, allowing the eye to wander in the purple vault of the night sky; from this falls a shower of flowers in the midst of which Venus and two cupids appear. Through the purple rhomboidal coffers, ivy tries to invade the cubicle from above with shoots with the fruit with three yellow stones. It was the plant of Dionysus, chewed by the Maenads to reach ecstasy: and the tambourines hanging from the obtuse corners of the rhombuses have the same function.

45. Cubicle (2), ceiling, S-E section. In the various yellow squares connecting the rhombuses (the valley and the wall) there are pairs of ducks. In the ceiling you can recognize timid attempts at a view from below up; in antiquity this dominant effect was only rarely achieved in the quadratures of Renaissance ceilings. Here Venus, tambourines and garlands are seen from the perspective and not in foreshortening, from below. The ceiling certainly predates the Neronian era, but very similar to the versatilia coenatium laquearia that changes with each plate (Sen., Ep., 90.15) and the rain of flowers poured out by Nero on the banqueters in the palace (Suet., Ner., 31).

47. Cubicle (2), ceiling, central vault. The Venus and the two cupids who flank her, the one to the E still held by the hand of his mother, the other to the W already released and ready to approach the earth, were modeled in stucco relief (which disappeared at the time of the excavation). The goddess was naked, the cloak worn on her shoulders fluttering behind her indicates the impact with the wind she encounters in her flight. To indicate that it is a shower of flowers, many are cut from the edges of the valley. Venus is represented here in the astral sense of the star Veneris (Cic., Nat. deor., 2.53), accompanied by Hesperus, the evening star (Noctifer), the elder cupid who is about to descend and by Phosphorus, the morning star (Lucifer) depicted by the cupid still attached to his mother. According to Aristotle (Meteor., p.53, 13 St.) Venus is in fact qupipavifs. The flowers seen from all angles are damask roses, primroses, daisies; the latter 389

The painted wall W of the fauces includes a purple plinth with plants, a middle area with three red panels, and the upper white area with a symmetrical structure with a picture with doors in the center and side aedicules, surmounted by paintings with birds. Structure and ornamental details, such as the vertical strips with yellow triangles alternating with green triangles, the internal strips of the red "handkerchief" panels, and the slender architecture with garlands in the upper area seem to come from the scheme used in the fauces of the House of M. Lucretius Fronto (V 4,11), decorated by an important workshop of painters of the III style. The black pilaster with mirrors made of three green parallel bars, which divides the fauces from the atrium, is also from the same workshop. The upper edge of the wall is marked by a moulded frame of white stucco, without moulded relief motifs.

18. Atrium (b), N-W section. To remedy the lack of space, a first floor was erected above the tablinum (d) and the corridor (k), with the introduction of a box staircase in the NW corner of the atrium. The side wall of the opus craticium coffin was reconstructed after excavation, with the use of concrete instead of horizontal and vertical wooden beams. The shelves of the steps of the staircase were made of limestone blocks and were lined with wooden boards. The storage room under the stairs is accessible by a door. The grazing light on the fresco of the O wall brings out the joint between the bridge of the middle area and that of the plinth, as well as the effect of the pressure exerted on the damp lime before the vertical and horizontal partitions were made.

19. Atrium (b). The columns that supported the four pitched roofs were not necessary for static reasons, as is shown by the many Tuscan atriums. Rather, they had a decorative purpose to give the atrium an air of grandeur. Of the circular marble table with three lion's paws, placed above the mouth of the cistern in the center of the N edge of the impluvium, the place of discovery is not known. Tables of this type are generally found placed in peristyles and in the rooms around the peristyle. G 8751

20. Atrium (b). The impluvium is built with fragments of amphora densely arranged like a knife, according to a technique attested in the second century B.C. C. in Delos, not very common in Italy. In Pompeii, besides this, there is only one other example, in the House of the Ancient Hunt (VII 4,57). It is a very solid technique: used for almost three centuries, the impluvium has only some slight restoration with marble slabs. Its very flattened kyma profile is a clue to the age of the system. The columns are set on a square lava stone.

21. Atrium (b). The base of the white marble fountain basin was found "in the middle of the impluvium", where it was exposed until 1979. The base and bottom of the basin are formed by acanthus leaves and the leaves of an aquatic plant. The seven animal heads carved under the outer edge of the basin constitute as many mouths for the outflow of the water supplied by the gush coming out of the perforated bottom of the basin (visible in fig. 20). The cosmic number seven (seven spheres, seven days, seven planets) often occurs in water games. The fountain could only function since Pompeii had been connected to the Serino aqueduct, wanted by Agrippa for his fleet stationed in Misenum.

22. Atrium (b). The mouth of the cistern dates back to the time of the construction of the house, as confirmed by the material used (travertine, not marble) and the fine grooved workmanship. The unpolished grooved surface allows the tip of the chisel to be seen, stepped. Inside, the hem is worn away by the passage of the rope. The mouth, a little off-center towards W on the S edge of the impluvium, is placed on a square lava stone (around which the ceramic fragments, arranged in a knife, of the impluvium are visible).
23. Atrium (b): the roof rebuilt with modern tiles and tiles, seen from above.

24. Atrium (b), floor, detail. The part intended for the walking of the papier-mâché floor dotted with white limestone tesserae, is bordered by two black and white mosaic frames, one around the impluvium and the other that leaves a large marginal cliff under the walls. The papier-mâché bottom is suitable for the austere atmosphere of the atrium (from ater, black) according to Latin grammarians. Many floor and wall decorations of the atriums of the time have a black background, in fact, and contrast with the bright floors of the peristyles.

40. Environment (i). The last period dates the installation of a kitchen in this room, first a cubicle divided into an alcove (section S) and an antechamber (section N). The back wall of the cubicle, frescoed on a white background, was decorated as a central aedicule with a vignette depicting an idyllic-sacral landscape, flanked by side panels with a crown hung by the bows with which it is tied. Typical decoration of secondary rooms, which has comparisons in houses I 8, 18, (6); I 10:4, (43); I, 12, 9, (3). It was probably the room of the atriensis or the procurator. 46. Tablinum (d), floor, section S-E. The cocciopesto floor, which was renovated in the first century AD, is located on a higher level than the level of the floor of the atrium, and has a design that became fashionable in the late Republican era: a network of squares and stars of eight rhombuses. The presence of colored marble tiles in the center of the squares prohibits such a high chronology, so it seems logical to date the construction to the phase of restoration in the III style of imitation. 22 AFS C1332

47. Tablinum (d), floor, central section. The opus sectile mat of palombino rhombuses, blackboard and green limestone, inserted in the cocciopesto, probably comes from a floor from the period of construction of the house. The resulting triangles are integrated with mosaic tiles; The black-and-white mosaic frame depicts flowering shoots coming out of a chalice-shaped crater placed in the center of the short sides and a pelta in the center of the long sides, while the corners are marked by an acanthus tuft or a stylized palmette tuft. The outer edge of the frame is "protected" by a two-ply braid. 22 AFS C1333

48. Tablinum (d), floor, threshold N. The threshold towards the garden portico follows the shape of a tabula ansata, whose ornamentation of white tesserae inserted in the cocciopesto reflects an architrave with square coffers filled with a square placed at the corner, containing a hexagon inscribed in a square; At the center of each hexagon is placed a colored marble tile. The travertine bases of the wooden door jambs have a square recess in which to insert the bronze ganghero (the one on the right is still in situ). Beyond the threshold appears the ancient cocciopesto floor of the portico, dotted with white limestone tiles as in the fauces and in the atrium.

49. Triclinium (e), S. You enter from the atrium through the door in the S wall. The triclinium room is painted almost entirely on a black background to create the initiatory atmosphere in which to welcome the banqueters. The decorative scheme of the opposite wall is repeated here despite the presence of the door, which apples with a central square and predella. In the choice of motifs, however, there is a hint of the door in the red predella to the W of it, which depicts a pair of sandals. At the top left, above the floor and the frame outlined in white, the corner of the vault lunette is visible. As often, the triclinium has two doors: one main and the other on the adjacent cubicle or corridor, so as not to leave the room through the entrance door.

50. Triclinium (e), S wall, W section of the door. The pair of sandals depicted at the foot of a small pillar, to which a torch is tied and which is surmounted by a lamp or urn, in the red predella next to the door, should perhaps refer to the practice of the banqueters to take off their sandals (soleas demere: Plaut., Truc., 2,4.16, and 2, 4.12) so as not to dirty the mattress of the tricliniary bed.

The place of the table is established by the carpet of colored marble tiles, inserted when the triclinium received its current decoration in the III style of imitation.

54. Triclinium (e), W wall, middle and upper area. From the garlands held by the parrots hang mystical cysts, with the lid half-open. The thyrsus consisting of a reed or other vegetable stem crowned by a bunch of ivy or a pine cone, is the scepter of Dionysus. The garlands which parrots hold in their beaks are presumably of sweet clover, like those which Osiris left at Nephtys, according to Plutarch (Mor., 356F, 366B); The cysts will contain the sacra or mysteria. 15 AFS C844

55. Triclinium (e), W wall, central section. The thòlos above the painting of Dionysus is the only one in the room: the corresponding section of the opposite wall is pierced by a window, and the structure in the center of the upper area in the short Se Nè walls has a triangular plan. The hemispherical roof of the thòlos is covered by a bellows net, while the dome is surmounted by what looks like a tripod. A clypeus hangs from the epistyle adorned with triglyphs and metopes with patera and supported by eight columns.

The cubicle was completely repaved with black and white mosaic with the use of yellow tiles, on the occasion of the renewal of the wall decoration in the III style of imitation. 78. Cubicle (f), wall E. The black plinth of the back wall, pierced by tunnels, has a tripartition typical of the III "classical" style, with a square placed at the corner in the central panel and a medallion placed in the center of a cross in the side panels. The central aedicule with a white background houses a figurative painting, the cupids in the red side panels are no longer legible. In the slender architecture of the upper area there are Dionysian followers. The white bezel has no traces of decoration.

79. Cubicle (f), wall E, section S, upper area. The rigid architectural scheme of the upper white area is softened by the play of flowering shoots, between which the fields of waste are filled with contrasting colors, and by the curtain hanging from the purple oscillum with a bust in profile, behind which stand the busts of a Maenad and a Satyr. The female figure standing to the right of the central branch has her head bandaged with the mitre, the headdress of the followers of Dionysus. Busts of Dionysian followers appear in the upper area of the triclinium (f) of the House of Jason (IX 5,18). A similar tent (mnapanétaopa) with the task of concealing the sacred of the mysteries, is painted in the exedra (e) of the nearby house I 7, 19 also there in the III style of imitation, perhaps by the same workshop.

7. Triclinium (b), N wall: detail of the cusped painting with Heracles in the garden of the Hesperides. The scene depicted above refers to the conclusion of the hero's feat who, according to two different versions of the myth - both of which the Pompeian painter seems to have been inspired by - alone or with the help of the Hesperides who tame the serpent, conquers the golden apples. The moment represented is not that of action but of rest; the club is almost abandoned, the bow and arrows hidden, while the hovering atmosphere is that of a melancholic idyll: despite the happy conclusion of the enterprise, despite the immortality conferred on them by the golden apples, the Hesperides are sad; one, whose figure is the least happy for the rendering of the volumes, weeps. This subject, widespread in reliefs, sarcophagi and coins, is known in painting in a few other examples (two from Pompeii, one from Herculaneum), in one of which, the one from V 2, 10 set against a landscape background.
